stem: Why is GNI per capita often adjusted for **purchasing power parity (PPP)**?

stem: A fictional country has a GNI of US\$27,300 million and a population of 21 million. Calculate its GNI per capita in US\$.

Describe **three** factors that affect a person's quality of life.

points.description: Health / access to health care and clean water.
Education / employment and income.
Safety and political stability / freedom / environmental quality / housing / family and community.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Quality of life depends on good health and access to clinics and safe water, on having education and a job, and on living in a safe, unpolluted environment with freedom.

stem: Explain why the HDI is a more useful measure of development than GNI per capita alone.

points.description: GNI per capita only measures income / wealth.
The HDI also includes health (life expectancy) and education (schooling).
Countries with similar incomes can differ greatly in health and education, so HDI gives a fuller picture.
But HDI still uses averages / misses inequality, freedom or environment (limitation noted).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: GNI per capita measures only average income. The HDI adds life expectancy and years of schooling, so it shows whether income is turned into better lives; countries with similar incomes can have very different HDIs. However, the HDI is still an average and ignores inequality and freedom.

explanation: Compare what each measures and note a limitation.

stem: 'No single indicator can measure development.' Evaluate this statement.

points.description: Economic indicators (GDP/GNI per capita) are easy to compare but measure only income.
Averages hide inequality between rich and poor, regions, rural and urban.
GNI misses the informal economy / subsistence; exchange rates distort without PPP.
Social indicators (life expectancy, infant mortality, literacy) show health and education outcomes.
Exceptions: some high-income countries have weaker social indicators, and some poorer ones have good health.
Composite indices (HDI) combine measures but still miss freedom, happiness, environment.
Judgement: agree - use a range of economic and social indicators / HDI plus others.

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: GNI per capita is the most widely used indicator because it is easy to compare, but it measures only average income. It hides inequality, so a country with a few very rich people can look developed while most people are poor, and it misses the informal economy and subsistence farming that are important in LICs. Social indicators such as life expectancy, infant mortality and literacy show whether people are healthy and educated, and they sometimes tell a different story: some oil-rich countries have high incomes but weaker education, while some poorer countries have long life expectancy. The HDI combines income, health and education, so it is more useful than any single indicator, but it is still an average and leaves out freedom, safety and the environment. The statement is therefore correct: development is many-sided, so a range of economic and social indicators should be used together.

hints: Discuss economic and social indicators, then judge.

stem:
Table 1 shows development indicators for three fictional countries (fictional data).

| Indicator | Country R | Country S | Country T |
|---|---|---|---|
| GNI per capita (US\$, PPP) | 2,100 | 15,800 | 54,000 |
| Life expectancy (years) | 61 | 76 | 82 |
| Infant mortality (per 1,000) | 48 | 12 | 3 |
| Adult literacy (%) | 66 | 94 | 99 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: How many times greater is Country T's GNI per capita than Country R's? Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the difference in life expectancy between Country T and Country R.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which country is most likely to be a LIC or lower-MIC?

options.rationale: S has middle values on every indicator.
T has the highest values on every indicator.
The indicators differ greatly.
Correct: lowest income, shortest lives, highest infant mortality.

parts.explanation: All four indicators place R lowest.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe the relationship between GNI per capita and infant mortality shown in Table 1, and suggest a reason for it.

points.description: As GNI per capita rises, infant mortality falls (negative relationship).
Uses data, e.g. R US\$2,100 and 48 per 1,000; T US\$54,000 and 3 per 1,000.
Reason: richer countries afford clinics, vaccinations, safe water, better diets.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Infant mortality falls as income rises: R (US\$2,100) has 48 per 1,000 but T (US\$54,000) only 3. Richer countries can afford clinics, vaccinations and safe water.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** limitations of using the data in Table 1 to compare the countries.

points.description: They are national averages that hide inequality / regional differences.
Informal economy not counted / data may be unreliable or out of date / miss freedom and environment.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The figures are averages that hide gaps between rich and poor, and income figures miss informal work.

explanation: This item practises comparing countries with indicators.
hints: Higher GNI and life expectancy, lower infant mortality.

options.content: It cannot be judged from income

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why Household 2 might have as good a **quality of life** as Household 1.
